solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Former lover aged, feeble in the head, hobbling

parts.note: aged means old

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of feeble is used

parts.note: someone hobbling is lame

explanation.surface: An unkind description of an ex who has grown old, weak-minded and unsteady on their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feeble in the head' reads as weak-minded, but it just means the first letter of feeble, F.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a past sweetheart: someone once loved, whose spark may still flicker.

clue.text: Expel, being in serious trouble

indicators.note: the letters wanted are being held inside the phrase serious trouble, across the word break

explanation.surface: Someone is thrown out because they have got into serious trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to throw someone out of a post or place is to remove them by force.

clue.text: After beginning to drink, finished port

indicators.note: After places the word for finished after the opening letter
the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only the start of drink is taken

parts.note: when something is finished it is over

explanation.surface: Someone starts drinking and has soon emptied the bottle of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like the drink, but it is the harbour town. DOVER is the English Channel ferry port in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Dover in Kent is Britain's busiest ferry harbour, facing France across the Channel.

clue.text: Very keen to keep partnership of many years

indicators.note: one word is made to keep the other within it, holding it in its middle

parts.note: being very keen on something is longing for it
in cricket a stand is a partnership between two batsmen

explanation.surface: Someone is eager to preserve a relationship that has lasted for decades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partnership' looks like the relationship in the surface, but in cricket a stand is a run-scoring partnership between two batsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym phrase: something that has existed for a long time is established over many years.

clue.text: In the mountains, male donkey meeting one female

parts.note: an ass is a donkey
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Up in the hills, a jack donkey meets a jenny.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains forming one mass, such as the Massif Central in France.

clue.text: Knock friends about

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the word for friends is read backwards

parts.note: pals are friends

explanation.surface: Someone pushes their mates around roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock ... about' reads as one verb, but 'about' is the turnaround signal for PALS.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a knock and a smack are both blows struck with the hand.

clue.text: Chicken, and two parts of a cow?

definitions.meaning: a breed of domestic hen from Livorno in Italy
a cow has a leg and a horn, so naming those two parts gives the word

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: put the words for two cow body parts together and you get the hen breed.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the Leghorn is a breed of domestic hen, famous as a prolific white egg-layer.

clue.text: Expecting page to have ruling

parts.note: regnant means reigning or ruling, as in a queen regnant

explanation.surface: Someone waits for a page boy to bring the official decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expecting' reads as waiting for something, but it means with child.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a woman who is expecting is carrying a baby, so she is with child.

clue.text: Focused, not trying to score boundaries?

definitions.meaning: a cricketer content to take singles, single runs, rather than hit fours and sixes to the boundary

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a boundary is a hit worth four or six runs; a batsman minded only to take singles is not chasing them.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: someone wholly intent on a single purpose is concentrated and determined.

clue.text: Small, divisible by two? It isn't

definitions.text: Small, divisible by two? It isn't

parts.note: a number that divides exactly by two is even

explanation.surface: A puzzle-like question about whether a little number splits into two, answered no.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer: a small number that would be EVEN, except 'It isn't', being odd.
explanation.definitionFit: The number described is a small odd number, one that cannot be halved into whole parts.

clue.text: Horrid English beach covered in this?

indicators.note: something horrid is ugly and misshapen, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A grim English beach with a pebbly surface that hurts the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horrid' turns ENGLISH into its seven letters rearranged; the beach then describes the result.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: many English beaches are covered in rounded pebbles rather than sand.

clue.text: Criticising for not wearing business suit?

definitions.meaning: choosing casual clothes rather than formal office wear

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that turning up without formal office clothes might itself earn a reprimand.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a severe reprimand or telling-off is a scolding, as in getting a dressing-down from the boss.

clue.text: Bare one buttock? Such spectacles!

definitions.meaning: to moon is to show one's bare bottom, so baring just one cheek is a half-sized version
glasses with half-lenses, for reading, shaped like a semicircle

explanation.walkthrough: Mooning means baring your backside as a prank; 'spectacles' plays on both an eyeful and eyeglasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-moon glasses have semicircular reading lenses that let the wearer look over the top.

clue.text: Attraction of a sound from the belfry heard

indicators.note: heard signals that the phrase is said aloud and the word sounding like it is entered

parts.note: a peal is the ringing of church bells from a bell tower

explanation.surface: Something charming about the bell-ringing from a church tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' says A PEAL is spoken aloud, giving a word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a thing's charm or allure is the pull it has on people.

clue.text: Tender university teacher ref upset

parts.note: prof is short for professor, a university teacher

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned over, so the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: ref is short for referee

explanation.surface: A sensitive academic upset a referee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective (sore), but it is the verb to offer. 'upset' turns REF into FER.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to tender something, like a resignation, is to offer or hold it out.

clue.text: American colonist working to make flag

parts.note: William Penn founded the colony of Pennsylvania
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: An early settler in America works at making a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long narrow pointed banner, once carried on a knight's lance.

clue.text: Divine messenger, a girl

parts.note: an angel is a messenger from God

explanation.surface: A girl is described as a heavenly envoy.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Angela is a common female first name, and crosswords use girl for any such name.

clue.text: Broken, folded, fled in battle

indicators.note: broken means smashed into pieces, so the letters of the words that follow are rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: In a battle an army collapsed, gave way and ran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges the letters of FOLDED, FLED and IN. Flodden (1513) was a battle in which England defeated Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the 1513 English victory over the Scots in Northumberland took place on this site.

clue.text: Gale wrecked rear of school, it's allowed

indicators.note: wrecked means ruined, so the letters of the storm word are rearranged
the rear of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of school is used

explanation.surface: A storm smashed up the back of a school building, and apparently that is permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' turns GALE into LEGA, and the rear of school adds L.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something permitted by the law of the land is lawful.

clue.text: Show excessive friendliness for young deer

definitions.meaning: to grovel or flatter someone in a servile way
a deer in its first year

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: to flatter obsequiously, and the noun for a baby deer, like Bambi.

clue.text: Crime: an insult, if this taken

definitions.meaning: people take umbrage, i.e. are hurt, at an insult

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: an insult is something at which you may 'take offence', so the missing word fills the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an unlawful act such as a misdemeanour, and the hurt feeling taken at a slight.

clue.text: I call myself divine — revolutionary doctrine

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: someone claiming divinity would say 'I am God', giving AM GOD

explanation.surface: A self-proclaimed god announces a radical creed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reads as radical, but it signals turning AM GOD back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a dogma is a fixed belief or principle laid down by an authority.

clue.text: Somewhat insane Roman emperor

indicators.note: Somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A description of a rather mad ruler of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is itself true: Nero was a famously unhinged Roman emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Nero ruled the Roman Empire from AD 54 to 68 and is notorious for cruelty.

clue.text: Chap handin' out instrument

parts.note: a chap is a man
handing out is doling, and with the final G dropped as the apostrophe shows it is dolin'

explanation.surface: A folksy picture of a fellow handing out something.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'handin'' signals a dropped G, so DOLING becomes DOLIN.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a mandolin is a small lute-like stringed instrument with paired strings, played with a plectrum.
